# Creating Your Creativity

### To create is a fundamental human instinct, yet why do we have such a hard time with it? Turns out, to create anything we must first create a sense of self. Machines can never do that.

Sometime last year, I came across a wonderful video clip where the Irish poet David Whyte shares how to keep walking through the metaphorical darkness of life where you are, for all intents and purposes, lost. He puts it more poetically and remarks that the only way to know that you’re on your path is when the path disappears. A longer version of the clip can be watched [here](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-GS2zAl3o1w) but the crucial part is where he narrates a poem by another poet, David Wagoner. The poem is titled “Lost” and draws from Native American wisdom. It goes like this,

***Lost***

*Stand still. The trees ahead and bushes beside you  
Are not lost. Wherever you are is called Here,  
And you must treat it as a powerful stranger,  
Must ask permission to know it and be known.  
The forest breathes. Listen. It answers,  
I have made this place around you.  
If you leave it, you may come back again, saying Here.  
No two trees are the same to Raven.  
No two branches are the same to Wren.  
If what a tree or a bush does is lost on you,  
You are surely lost. Stand still.*   
*The forest knows where you are.*  
*You must let it find you.  *
  
This immediately reminded me of the Brihadaranyaka Upanishad which is one of the ten principal Upanishads, where Aranyaka refers to a forest. The name of the text takes a whole new meaning when you consider the fact that it has to do with the nature of self and our highest preoccupations such as knowledge, ethics, philosophy, metaphysics, complexities of human experiences, and the like. While the text is infinitely deep and profound, the insight for me here was about how much of our personal journeys can feel like the wilderness of a forest.

Today, it’s easier than ever before to make the mistake of taking our outward life to be the only reality. In this age of individualism which is turbo-charged by our tools of instant gratification, we may think that the only journey that matters is the one that the world sees us go through— achievements, life milestones, resources, personalities, and so on. But this poem and of course the Upanishads hint at something much more profound. They tug us to go within ourselves; to sharpen our senses so deeply and precisely that we can no longer tell the difference between the journey within and without. This is a journey that we cannot see, touch, or strategise our way through because it does not yet exist like a map. It has no well-trodden path, no signage, no milestones that tell us where or how far the destination is. Instead, this journey is full of hidden threats, deceptions, and exhaustion. Which is why, it requires absolute stillness which gives us the ability to listen, think, and act decisively as we take one step after another on this journey.

To me, this has a profound implication about what it means to create. To create anything— wealth, knowledge, art, or even life itself— is a journey of persisting long and hard and alone despite not knowing what it may yield (or if it will even yield anything at all). So what makes us persist still? What is the invisible force that we cannot comprehend but goads us along all the same? Why does life insist on itself despite the utter darkness?

We can resort to certain tailor-made answers for these questions. It is our subconscious mind, our Karma, our destiny that pushes us forward. But if it were so simple, we could go along for an eternity and never become aware of the veil that separates the known from the unknown. This veil is important because it marks our life before and after coming to a new consciousness. The lifting of this veil is also somewhat of a catastrophic event because when the unknown makes itself known to us, it shatters our conception of what we think we know. It forces us to confront the unknown without giving us a way to do so. It leaves it to us to find our path through it.

Subscribe

Yet, what is this pathless path really made of? It is made of our own self. When we walk through the wilderness of the forest, it is our self that starts to take birth. This self is not the one of names and labels that the outer world recognises but something much more subtle yet more powerful. It is made of our essence, i.e., imprints that our soul carries and wants to manifest through the ego. But why should the cosmos care about the desires of our soul? Well, perhaps because our soul is not so different than the cosmos itself. The journey of our self is something we create as we go but it is not just us who goes through it. It appears as if the entire Universe is going through it too. As if the cosmos is experiencing itself through us while we experience ourselves through the cosmos.

Creation is always a process of expressing a felt unknown. Whether it is felt as a desire for abundance, wisdom, beauty, or a sheer continuity of life, it forces us to apply ourselves no matter how much of it feels like being lost in a forest. In this context, I want to share a few lines by David Whyte from a recent [Substack](https://substack.com/home/post/p-196827160) post by him where he has written about the nature of creativity. He writes,

*“Creativity demands choosing longing over belonging: that choice asks us to risk losing grip with what makes sense—to drop into a state where the familiar self cannot follow a known path.* *To follow the path of creativity is to stay in the unknown long enough for it to become aliveness—and to shape that aliveness into forms of beauty and life-changing insight—the gift of being given new eyes or ears for this world or even a new mind for an imagined future.*”

In other words, to create is to evolve in your soul. And while the nature of our soul remains eternal and universal, it is important to bear in mind that it manifests in a certain circumstance. When we talk about AI art and knowledge, we miss out on these implications because we do not take into consideration that anything that we create is a manifestation of the cosmos itself. Machines cannot have desires, struggle to fulfil them, and eventually let go of them. They cannot have a soul and their consciousness cannot evolve.

But perhaps there is a silver lining to the AI age after all. More than anything else, it will force us to confront the unknown within and without. In doing so, it will force us to create ourselves all over again from the ground up. Which is why, we must create whatever we can without fearing the deep forests that lie in our pathless paths.
